The honest version of Aguirre, the Wrath of God starts by giving up the comforting part. The film is an international co-production between West Germany, Mexico, and Peru. The film used a minimalist approach to story and dialogue to evoke madness and folly, counterpointed by the lush but unforgiving Amazonian jungle.

Strip Aguirre, the Wrath of God of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Although loosely based on what is known of the historical Lope de Aguirre, Herzog acknowledged years after the film's release that its storyline is a work of fiction. Some of the people and situations may have been inspired by missionary Gaspar de Carvajal's account of an earlier Amazonian expedition, although Carvajal never accompanied Aguirre on any of his expeditions.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Aguirre, the Wrath of God shows exactly where that breaks. They had differing views as to how the role should be played, and they clashed throughout filming; Kinski's rage terrorized both the crew and the locals who were assisting the production. The film was shot entirely on location, and has itself become famous for its difficulties.

What looks like free choice in Aguirre, the Wrath of God is older than choice itself. During an arduous five-week shoot in the Peruvian rainforest, Herzog filmed on and near tributaries of the Amazon River in the Ucayali region. The cast and crew climbed mountains, cut through heavy vines to open routes to the various jungle locations, and rode treacherous river rapids on rafts built by local craftworkers.

Nobody designed the part of Aguirre, the Wrath of God you experience — it was inherited. Aguirre opened to widespread critical acclaim, and quickly developed a large international cult following. It was given an extensive arthouse theatrical release in the United States in 1977, and remains one of the director's best-known films.

Every serious account of Aguirre, the Wrath of God eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Several critics have declared the film a masterpiece, and it has appeared on Time magazine's list of "All Time 100 Best Films". On Christmas Day, 1560, several scores of Spanish conquistadors under Gonzalo Pizarro and two hundred native slaves march down from the newly conquered Inca Empire into the Amazon rainforest in search of the fabled El Dorado.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Aguirre, the Wrath of God — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. The men, clad in half armor, pull cannons down narrow mountain paths and through dense, muddy jungle. On New Year's Eve, Pizarro orders a group of forty men to build rafts and scout down the river.

The selfish-gene reading of Aguirre, the Wrath of God makes it less romantic and far more precise. If they do not return to the main party within one week with news of what lies beyond, they will be considered lost. Pizarro chooses Don Pedro de Ursúa as the commander of the expedition, Don Lope de Aguirre as his second-in-command, portly nobleman Don Fernando de Guzmán to represent the Spanish crown, and Brother Gaspar de Carvajal to bring the word of God.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. Accompanying the expedition, against Pizarro's better judgment, are Ursúa's mistress, Doña Inés, and Aguirre's teenage daughter Flores. One of the four rafts gets caught in an eddy while traveling through river rapids, and the others are unable to help free it.

The feeling that Aguirre, the Wrath of God means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. That night, gunfire erupts on the trapped raft; in the morning, the men on board are found slain by arrows from Indigenous tribesmen, with three missing. Ursúa wants the bodies to be brought back to camp for burial.

Nothing in Aguirre, the Wrath of God was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Knowing this would slow down the expedition, Aguirre suggests to a soldier, Perucho, that the cannon is rusty and needs firing. Perucho aims at the raft, destroying it and abandoning the bodies in the river.

The psychology underneath Aguirre, the Wrath of God is simpler and older than the story on top. During the night, the remaining rafts are swept miles off course by the rising river. Time has run out for the scouting mission, and Ursúa decides that they must return to Pizarro's camp.

Behind Aguirre, the Wrath of God sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. Aguirre leads a mutiny against Ursúa, telling the men that untold riches await them ahead, and reminding them that Hernán Cortés won an empire in Mexico by disobeying orders. Ursúa orders Aguirre arrested but is shot and restrained by the mutineers.

The nihilist does not deny Aguirre, the Wrath of God — he only refuses to flatter it. Aguirre nominates Guzmán as the new leader of the expedition and has his men renounce their loyalty to the Crown, proclaiming Guzmán "emperor" of El Dorado. Ursúa is sentenced to death in a show trial but  Guzmán unexpectedly commutes the sentence.

What culture calls destiny in Aguirre, the Wrath of God is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Aguirre remains the true leader of the mutiny, so oppressive and terrifying that few protest his leadership. Knowing that some of the soldiers are still loyal to Ursúa, Aguirre ignores her.

The genes do not care about Aguirre, the Wrath of God; they care about copies. The expedition breaks up the rafts to make a single large one and continues on downriver. An Indigenous couple approaching peacefully by canoe are captured by the explorers, and when the man expresses confusion upon being presented with a Bible, Carvajal personally kills them for blasphemy.

Take away the meaning and Aguirre, the Wrath of God still functions — that is the disturbing part. Guzmán insists on being fed first while the other men starve and has the expedition's only remaining horse pushed off the raft because it annoys him; soon afterwards he is found dead near the raft's privy. Aguirre proclaims himself leader and has Ursúa taken ashore to be hanged.

The unconscious does not argue with Aguirre, the Wrath of God; it simply acts first. He orders an attack on an Indigenous village to obtain food, resulting in several men being killed. On the raft, the group of slowly starving, feverish men begin disbelieving everything they see even as arrows are fired at them.

Aguirre, the Wrath of God feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. The group stares in disbelief at a wooden ship perched in the highest branches of a tall tree. Aguirre orders that it be brought down and refurbished, but Carvajal refuses.

The bleak reading of Aguirre, the Wrath of God is also the most testable one. In a series of attacks by unseen assailants, all of the remaining crew except Aguirre, including Flores, are shot dead with arrows. Monkeys overrun the raft as Aguirre deliriously imagines conquering the New World and founding an incestuous dynasty with his slain daughter.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Aguirre, the Wrath of God. The idea for the film began when Herzog borrowed a book on historical adventurers from a friend. After reading a half-page devoted to Lope de Aguirre, the filmmaker became inspired and immediately devised the story.

The self that experiences Aguirre, the Wrath of God is a committee, not a king. He fabricated most of the plot details and characters, although he did use some historical figures in purely fictitious ways. Much of the script was written during a 200-mile (320 km) bus trip with Herzog's football team.

Reproduction explains more of Aguirre, the Wrath of God than any philosophy dares to admit. His teammates got drunk after winning a game and one vomited on several pages of Herzog's manuscript, which he immediately threw out the window. Herzog claims that he cannot remember what he wrote on these pages.

Once you see Aguirre, the Wrath of God as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Later in the screenplay, Aguirre and his men find a boat and the long-dead remains of Orellana's soldiers. Further down the river, they discover another ship lodged in the treetops.

The story Aguirre, the Wrath of God tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. In the screenplay, Aguirre and others explore the boat but find no sign of Orellana or his men. Herzog ultimately eliminated any such references to Orellana's expedition from the film.

Meaning is not found in Aguirre, the Wrath of God — it is manufactured for it. The sequence with the boat caught in the upper branches of a tree remains, but as filmed it seems to be simply a hallucinatory vision. The end was actually the raft going out into the open ocean and being swept back inland, because for many miles you have a counter-current, the Amazon actually goes backwards.

The cold light on Aguirre, the Wrath of God leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. This ending was eventually adapted for Cobra Verde, Herzog's final film with Kinski. The two had met many years earlier when the then-struggling young actor rented a room in the same boarding house as Herzog's family, and Kinski's often terrifying antics during the three months he lived there left a lasting impression on the young Herzog.

Aguirre, the Wrath of God did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. From the beginning of the production, Herzog and Kinski argued about the proper manner to portray Aguirre. Kinski wanted to play a "wild, ranting madman", but Herzog wanted a "quieter, more menacing" portrayal.

The honest version of Aguirre, the Wrath of God starts by giving up the comforting part. In order to get the performance he desired, Herzog would deliberately infuriate Kinski before each shot and wait for the actor's anger to "burn itself out" before rolling the camera. On one occasion, irritated by the noise from a hut where members of the cast and crew were playing cards, the explosive Kinski fired three gunshots at it, blowing the tip off of one extra's finger.

Strip Aguirre, the Wrath of God of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Kinski subsequently decided to leave the jungle location over Herzog's refusal to fire a sound assistant, only changing his mind after Herzog threatened to shoot first Kinski and then himself. This incident is parodied in the 2004 film Incident at Loch Ness, which Herzog co-wrote.

The film was made for $370,000 (equivalent to $2,847,852 in 2025), with one-third of the budget going towards Kinski's salary. It was filmed on location in the Peruvian rainforest, Machu Picchu (the stone steps of Huayna Picchu), and on the Amazon River tributaries of the Ucayali region.

What looks like free choice in Aguirre, the Wrath of God is older than choice itself. Aguirre was shot in five weeks following nine months of pre-production planning. The film was shot in chronological order, as Herzog believed the film crew's progress on the river directly mirrored that of the explorers' journey in the story.
